utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. Hvalkof. Could I remind you of the oath or the affirmation which you took on the first day which is still in force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hvalkof, my name is Goran Rodic, and on behalf of Defence counsel, I would put to you a few questions relating to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many years you were an active-duty military person in the Danish army.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1955 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1996 you retired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you retire with the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me more details about your experience and the level of training for the use of the RPG 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trained at the infantry sergeants school at 81-millimetre mortars and 120-millimetre mortars. I had been a section commander as a sergeant, a platoon commander as a lieutenant, first in 81-millimetres and as a lieutenant both in 81- and 120-millimetres mortars platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me for how long in total you were involved with mortar units, including your training period, so in total, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1955 until the end of the year 1960 dealing permanently with mortar units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I presume that during these five years you were involved in lots of exercises of firing mortars?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also presume that given your training and experience you can easily recognise the incoming or outgoing mortars and shells?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. It depends on the distance you are from the incoming and outgoing mortars. It's difficult when you are sitting far away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately which would be the distance that can make it difficult for you differentiate and establish the trajectory of those missiles.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking of incoming, I would say I have to be -- it's pretty close. You can hear the sound, in a couple of hundred metres, maybe. But in this case, I -- the mortars -- if there were mortar shells - I cannot prove - landing in Dubrovnik, for example, they were too far away for me to distinguish what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July 1957, you were a lieutenant -- you were a sergeant. In 1975, you were a major, and you arrived in Split in 1992 also as a major.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I was back in Split -- in the Split area as a major in 1992, yes. But that was in the UNPROFOR mission in 1992. But I was down in the Split area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the area of Split in 1991 as well?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 1968 and 1991, you participated in a number of UN missions as a representative of the Danish army. Can you just enumerate for me the countries where you served.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually -- actually started in 1956, but probably from 1961, I was serving in the UNEF I Force in the Gaza Strip for a bit more than six months as a platoon commander. I was then serving in UNSO United Nations II Supervision Organisation at that time in brackets P for Palestine from spring 1965 until the -- after the end of the six-day war in 1967, with a break of about three to four months when I was sent to the United Nations in the Pakistan observation mission in connection with the war between India and Pakistan where I served in Rajastan, Sindh, and Punjab. And I returned again to UNSO from 1971 and in 1971. In 1972, I served in UNMO keeping -- United Nations, India, Pakistan -- military observer group, basically in Kashmir. In 1979 and 1982 for a three-year period I served in the -- again in UNMO in Kashmir. And during those days, I both served as the officer in charge of field station around in the area and as an operation officer in the headquarters in several periods. I served then in the ECMM, as you have been informed already, from -- actually starting officially in Zagreb on the 15th of October, 1991, and returning around Christmas 1991 to Denmark, because my wife was ill. And then I was asked again to go to the -- as an UNMO, that means United Nations Military Observer attached to UNPROFOR, the United Nations Protection Force in your country, or in ex-Yugoslavia, and I was there from end July until 1st -- I think 1st August, end July 1992 to 1st of August or 31st of July. I can't remember the date exactly until 1993. Anyway, for one year, in 1993. And then I returned to my country and proceeded working both for the army and as a vice-principal at a secondary school until my retirement from both duties. And that's the end of my life in that respect. I hope that will please you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what was the principle that you operate on. Did you offer your services for these missions, or was any other criteria applied. If you just tell us briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time my company was sent to the Gaza Strip, 1961. The second time, I applied. That was for UNSO. And then I have -- I think I applied the next time, but the following times I was requested to go. For example, when I -- sorry, I forgot one year. I think I forgot my Iraq/Iran business. That was -- I'd forgotten that one. I gave descriptions for you. I'm - no, I'm getting old. From 1998, early August, until 1990, I was serving in Iran and Iraq, also as a military observer where I was in charge of the area -- the southern part of Kurdistan, Sulaymaniya including the -- in that area, first army corps. It was sort of on the ad Halapsa [phoen], the Gas City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me about your ECMM mission in Yugoslavia. Did you voluntarily apply for that mission?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived in Zagreb on the 15th of October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who received you in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was met by a manager who was already serving at the headquarters, and then I was -- I came late in the night or in the evening. And I was -- then the following day, along with other newcomers, reached by the operational staff in the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who briefed you and who did they tell you about the situation in the Former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave us a general briefing of the work, the difficulties, the problems, and what the situation was like. It was not easy, it was not pleasant, and we were informed about the -- that we were there, as I mentioned the other day, we were there to be present and try to make the two sides, opposing parties, meet and negotiate. And in general, that we -- the basic idea was that the two sides should negotiate themselves and we should sort of assist and try to make it work. And then in case there were -- we found there was something essential we had to add, we had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you. This is a different issue, and I'll ask about that later. What I did ask you was: What were you told about the situation in the former Yugoslavia? You were coming to a country. You were briefed about the situation there. Who briefed you? What problems did they tell you existed in the country?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again that I was briefed by the operational staff in the headquarters, and they told me the situation was difficult, you had the fighting. They told me about the JNA enclaves, for example, in Croatia. I was informed about the troubles down in the Knin area. I was informed about the situation in Dubrovnik, in Vukovar, Osijek area. And if you're asking me about all the details at that briefing, I'm sorry, I can't give you an answer. But it was a difficult situation where people were sort of fighting and people were in trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Yugoslavia before that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you say that again, please -- oh, sorry, I can see it now. Yes, I had been to Yugoslavia once before in 1967, when I came back after the six-day war. I drove with my wife through Greece and passed, by the way, Dubrovnik and Split. And that's the only time I have been to Yugoslavia before -- oh, sorry. I've been there once more as -- I passed through Yugoslavia from north to south from Greece to Austria [sic] in 1960 in November. It was just straight through; no sight seeing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1991, did anyone inform you about the social and political system of the country that you arrived in about the state organs, institutions, and things like that? Did you have any detailed information about that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were informed briefly about the -- well, the -- we were, for example, informed about the business where we were dealing, for example, with presidents who were apparently mayors and we were informed about -- as how the mission -- the Yugoslavian army enclaves in the area and in general, as I said, what people knew about the Dubrovnik and Knin -- in that area, in my case particularly. A general idea of what -- how the situation was, and it was, let's say, not normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you how many republics there were in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that before I came, but I think they told me. It's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what was the only, at the time, legitimate armed force in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was only in my opinion -- well, there was only -- there was the army -- the army we were dealing with was the JNA. And then you had the Croatian forces, which they were called ZNG as far as I remember. But you had the JNA army and then you had the Croats in -- who were fighting for their cause. And I think they were called ZNG. I'm sorry if that is wrong but -- you saw Croatian armed forces, yes, in the area. And we knew they were there and I was told they were there, and we could see them. When I was along evacuating the Borongaj - I think that was the name - barracks, with the JNA forces down to Karlovac, there were Croatian forces, you could see them in the distance from the roof where we evacuated the troops. They were there and I was told they were there -- actually, how they were organised in detail, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't hear the translation. Did anyone tell you that there were paramilitary formations in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were paramilitary forces, both in Croatia and in JNA-controlled areas. I was informed about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of paramilitary forces whose name -- abbreviated name was HOS and which were attached to the Croatian party of right.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heart that, yes. I haven't talked to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that the ZNG, or the Croatian -- the national guard corps was also a paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. We were taught about Croatian forces and the JNA. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time were you aware under the SFRY constitution was the legal armed force in the then-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SFRY, would you please verify that abbreviation, please. I can't remember I've seen the abbreviation. I would like to know exactly what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the country in which you arrived on the 15th of October, 1991, and it's full name was Social Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry about that. I'll just go back and read here. So what do you mean when you say: "At that time were you aware under the SFRY constitution was the legal armed force in the then-Yugoslavia" -- you mean that they were the legal armed forces in ex-Yugoslavia or in then-Yugoslavia. Yeah, you can say -- well, they were legal armed forces in my opinion, yes. It was -- in my opinion, nothing -- and I have not heard that it was unlegal. Nobody heard it was unlegal. It was legal according to me and according to people. I don't think anybody ever sort of tried to instruct me that was a legal force; it was obvious it was legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who you are talking about now, which army.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are talking about the -- I'm trying to answer your question about the JNA of the Social Republic of Yugoslavia army. And if that -- well, I just don't understand what you mean, except that of course it was a legal army, a legal army forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your experience as a soldier, were all the other armies on the ground then, apart from the JNA, illegal or paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not and was not up to me to decide. I was there to monitor and help to assist to achieve some sort of peace between two opposing parties. If you do that as a military observer, a peacekeeper, you're not concerned about what people -- it might be illegal elements in India or Iraq or anywhere. You are concerned about parting these groups. It's a political question about if they're legal or not. And it's not up to me as a military observer or an EC monitor to decide whether these people were legal or not. They were there. The fact they were there and I was dealing with that fact. If they were legal, it's none of my business. So if you want the Danish opinion about that, you will have to go ask my politicians, my government, or the EC -- or now EU.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Adrian Stringer?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An observer from Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't ring a bell. I may have met him. I've met hundreds of people, thousands. I can't remember his name, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Colm Mangan, on Irish colonel? Did you see his reports? He was also a monitor?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I might have met him. I don't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Lars Brolund?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come to Yugoslavia before you did?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my knowledge he was there when I came, yes, I'm nearly sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lars Brolund returned from the mission in Dubrovnik just before you arrived in Zagreb. And Colonel Mangan was in the same team?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Lars Brolund, as your fellow countryman from Denmark, tell you about the situation in Croatia and Dubrovnik and about his experiences?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never really met before down in Split. And I hardly saw him because of different work before we ended up in Dubrovnik together, so we didn't discuss that. I only saw his reports and got information about him, which I had to as a head of the Danish delegation. But actually, we never discussed Dubrovnik as much person-to-person in Danish before we were sitting down in the mess. And then he was an excellent support, I'll say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which sides signed the memorandum of the presence of the ECMM of the 13th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be wrong of me to sit here and say yes, I can tell exactly who signed that. I would rather not. But I can just say -- and if I say something, it's -- no, that would be unfair because you want all the details and I can't give all the details clearly because I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the Yugoslav side, this memorandum was signed by representatives of the federal secretariat for foreign affairs of Slovenia and Croatia and the Ambassador and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Holland, Kristjen Kroner [phoen] signed on behalf of the international community.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say what I said before, I am not sure and for that reason I will not answer -- I cannot answer. And if you ask again in a different way, the answer will be the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you acquainted with the contents of the memorandum of the ECMM of the 13th of July, 1991? You can reply briefly with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were acquainted with the contents?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it at the time, but you can -- are not going to force me into telling all the details of what I read at the time, because that was a part of the briefing. And I can't help say now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: But may I say another word, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I can't see what this has got to do with the case and the reason why I have been chased down here, all this now. This is just my remark, that's the way I feel, and I don't like to be fooled around in a way in which I don't understand what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, if you would just answer the questions put to you by counsel. It's for us to determine when that goes too far from the mark, and we will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, isn't one -- isn't that memorandum one of the basic documents on the basis of which the ECMM was active in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it now clear to you why I put that question?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the basic mandate of the ECMM was to assist, number one, in stabilising the cease-fire to put an end to the siege of the JNA barracks; and secondly, to oversee the suspension of the declaration of independence over a three-month period, and this was agreed upon by the parties receiving the mission?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you are right. But again, I read all this in 1991. I have not looked at it since. It seems very right what you are saying, but I cannot remember the details. I was sent down there to do a job, which I did, and nobody has criticised me for what I did according to the orders I had. So all these details -- I cannot remember all the exact wording, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Hvalkof, I am trying to make my questions clear and precise. Please answer clearly and precisely, because time is very precious. Is it correct that this memorandum on the mission of the European Community was to ensure the implementation of the Brioni declaration of the 7th of July, 1991, which was passed with the presence and active participation of the ministerial troika of the European community?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Slovenia and Croatia undertook in that declaration to lift the siege of all the units and facilities of the JNA and to re-establish the previous border regime, and all this within a period of 24 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Is that short enough?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the representatives of Croatia and Slovenia undertook especially to refrain from any one-sided acts of violence and to start negotiations on the future of the SFRY and the peaceful resolution of the crisis in the spirit of the Helsinki declaration and the Paris charter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been written -- I cannot remember it. I may have been; it sounds reasonable. But I have told you, I cannot remember what was written in details in these papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it known to you that immediately after this, there was a series of attacks on JNA units, on JNA conveys, that JNA property was looted, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the mandate of the ECMM was strengthened and extended on the 2nd of September, 1991, by the memorandum on the monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was strengthened. I don't know the -- can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that you could evaluate and investigate breaches of the cease-fire, as agreed on the 2nd of September, 1991, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- for sure I know we could evaluate and investigate breaches of a cease-fire, yes. Date is out of my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to that agreement, were all paramilitary and irregular units to be disarmed and disbanded, including the reserve forces of the Croatian National Guard, the ZNG, that was Article 1 of the memorandum of the 2nd of September, 1991, which you read?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details of that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the government of the SFRY in June 1991 initiated proceedings before the constitutional court to the effect that the founding of the ZNG, as a professional armed formation, was an unconstitutional and illegal act by the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Whether he knows this legal fact or not, it really doesn't make a difference, his knowledge of constitutional issues of what's going on in mid-1991 in Yugoslavia -- in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There may be much in that, but this is an attempt which I can understand to develop an aspect of the Defence case through a witness who was a significant representative of the monitoring mission, and I think it only reasonable to allow it to continue. That doesn't mean that I do not appreciate the point you make.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you just give me time to read this again, what you said last. Thank you. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that after your arrival in Zagreb on the 16th of October, the constitutional court issued a decision on the illegality and unconstitutionality of the founding of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your mission consistently insist on disarming and the disbanding of the ZNG and other paramilitary formations in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what the mission insisted on. It was not, let's say, on my level where I was working. But my main job was to deal with cease-fire violations and negotiations. And exactly when the mission insisted on this and that was not an essential part of my life and my work in that respect down there. And I cannot remember all these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the mission worked on this at all pursuant to the agreement and the memorandum that was signed?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that the mission worked very hard on all lines on whatever their conditions were. They did their utmost at the head of the mission; I know that for sure. But they were working hard on their level and I was working hard on my level. But I know they worked hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Zagreb, do you know that at that time JNA forces were exposed to attacks in their barracks and bases in Croatia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were fighting around several barracks and garrisons and various places, Croatia here; that is correct. Who was starting what and when, I wouldn't know and that's probably difficult. But there were fightings around the JNA-controlled areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were in Zagreb, the JNA, as the legal army, was it out in the streets or was it in its barracks?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In its barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the members of the ZNG and other paramilitary formations, did you see them on the streets of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have seen a single soldier in Zagreb, but very few. And I will have to remind you, I was only there for a few days, and during the few days I was out, for example, down to this Karlovac business, I have seen and I've mentioned before --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw ZNG soldiers a distance from the route, along the road, motorway, what have you from Zagreb to Karlovac, I saw ZNG soldiers, but actually they were not -- in the few times I was in the streets of Zagreb, I didn't see any -- I might have seen one, but it was not something you really saw. What I saw -- I would again remind you, I was only there for a few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, are you trying to tell me that the one or two ZNG members you saw were blocking the barracks in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any blocking barracks in Zagreb. When I was walking a few short times in Zagreb, it was because I had an hour or two off. I was not near barracks. And when I say I might have seen a soldier who I -- a uniformed man, I didn't even know if I had seen one, which unit, which army, or anything, except that I would presume when he walked in the streets of Zagreb he would be a Croatian soldier of some sort. But they were not -- in the few times I was there, very -- not hardly any -- well, I may have seen one. Civilians I saw lots of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me briefly, on your arrival in Zagreb, do you know whether there were any attacks on the facilities and barracks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if there were attacks. There was shooting in Zagreb, and mostly at nighttime. But if that was an attack or something else, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly how many days you spent in Zagreb, bearing in mind that on the 28th of October the work of the regional centre in Split started?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Split on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you spent a week in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately a week, yeah -- well, it takes a bit of time also to move down to Split, and you could not go the normal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly but surely, Mr. Hvalkof. So know nothing about the exchanges, about the number and consequences of the attacks on the JNA in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that area, because I was not investigating it, I didn't read the reports, I was doing other things. And I can't tell you anything about something I have not taken part in. The only thing I took part in was evaluating the JNA out of the Borongaj barracks down to Karlovac. That's the only time I saw JNA; that's the only time I saw Croatian military forces, when I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yourself that in Zagreb you read the reports from various parts of Croatia where your monitors were stationed, and that you familiarised yourself with the situation from Karlovac to Dubrovnik. You said that you followed the situation in Vukovar and all this through the reports of your monitors. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say so. I said that I was briefed on the first day about the general situation, and yesterday I said that the day before I went to Split I read whatever was available about the Split area of responsibility. I did that that day, and I -- the other stuff I did not read. That was pouring through my ears in various actions of different nationalities in the headquarters, so that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you did not see and did not know, for example, that in Zagreb the JNA barracks were blockaded, that somebody was attacking the barracks, shooting at the army, there was no need for monitors, there was no need to separate any sides or negotiate with anyone. Is this what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. But I don't see that sort of thing, and it was not -- I was not a party for that particular duty, I was not ordered to deal with that. It's doesn't mean that. I'm telling you what I saw and what I didn't saw. What the mission did or what other monitors did and were ordered to do was none of my business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you not only whether you saw this, but whether you heard about it, and you are constantly denying it.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying anything. I am just telling -- I'm supposed to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tell the truth, and I told the truth. I wouldn't think of telling nothing but the truth. So I'm telling you what I experienced. And I heard about -- I heard -- now and then I could hear shooting at night, yes, but I was not involved in the cases. And people who probably were involved were dealing with this and making their report, and it was an operational matter. I was not part of that show. I was supposed to go somewhere else. And I don't waste people's time by going and asking fun -- questions about something I'm not dealing with. Don't force me to tell you something I don't want to, because I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that yesterday you testified about the documents from Dubrovnik at the time when you were not in Dubrovnik at all and when it was not even an assigned duty to you at the time. Is that correct? Can you just please reply with yes or no. I don't need lengthy explanations.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I need a lengthy explanation -- or more than yes or no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm kindly asking you -- I'm asking the questions, and I formulate them in such a manner that I don't need elaborate explanations. I'm kindly asking you not to waste my time in that manner. Therefore, is it true that yesterday you testified about written documents referring to Dubrovnik while you were not in Dubrovnik, or you sent anyone to carry out that assignment. Instead, you just happened to be in Zagreb and you were in a position to read those reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified about those documents because I had read them, and I was asked by the Prosecutor if I had seen them and yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any other documents, apart from those referring to Dubrovnik, hidden from you while you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know if anybody had hidden it? I wouldn't have seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that you haven't seen any other document relating to the problems in Croatia, except those from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes, that is correct. There were lots of documents and what have you. We got a general briefing, as I said before, and I was allowed to read -- I was asked to read whatever was available and there was time for about the Split/Dubrovnik/Sibenik area before I went down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, in your country, since you used to be an active-duty military person, would any attacks on the regular army -- would be deemed as terrorist attacks under your laws? And this is also part of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually we are not operating with terrorist attack, but an attack in -- on my country would be deemed as an action of war. But we are not operating with terrorists. I wouldn't know. We haven't done so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I say that we agree on the point that your position of the head of the -- deputy head of the regional centre of the ECMM in Split was a high-ranking position within the mission?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me to decide or have an opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please help us so that we can arrive at an opinion and to evaluate that, because as far as I know there was a head of the whole mission in Zagreb, that was the Dutch Ambassador. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many regional centres of the ECMM existed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other day I said I was -- I could not remember -- I was not aware if there were any others, but to the best of my knowledge there were not at the time when I left the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the Split mission headquarters, you remained until Christmas of 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is something more than two months. Right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more than two months, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to quote one section from tab 42, which contains your description and/or your perception of the situation in the country where you were deployed, and that is on the first page beneath your photograph. And I'm talking about this passage: "Since readers should really know the background and the history of Yugoslavia, I will just say briefly what I believe that the main reasons for conflict between Croatia and Serbia (represented here by the federal army, known colloquially as the JNA). Item 1, centuries of ethnic and religious disagreements; item 2, establishment of military Croatia within Austria-Hungary creating a Serb minority; item 3, the mass extermination of Serbs in Nazi Croatia during the Second World War; and item 4, the part of the Serb leaders and generals, they would loose their own privileges the richer provinces into the north and access to the sea." Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote that after I had been down there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, that was in early May 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of the mission dealing with Serbia and Croatia, or were you deployed within the mission in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 15th October 1991 and Christmas 1991.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was dealing with Croatia and Serbs and the JNA -- or I was deployed on the Croatian side, yes, in Split. It wasn't the Croatian side, if you will know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you working for the Croatian side then?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a neutral man posted on that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, Mr. Hvalkof. Can you please explain to me in more details what do you mean by the "federal army known colloquially as the JNA"?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explaining to my countrymen what it was, and why I think I probably later on used the abbreviation "JNA," to my countrymen, the readers of this, so people would know because it was an official term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also informed your fellow countrymen about the fact that the federal army represented Serbia. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably did so, but I can see now what you say, what I should have said it was Yugoslavia. And I will admit that was an error. The federal army represented Yugoslavia, yes. It was a wrong thing to put there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In order not to go through all these four items that I had just read to you, can you please tell me: Don't you think that these statements of yours are pretentious, given the scope of knowledge that you had about Yugoslavia and its history, or do you really believe that you can provide some serious arguments for these conclusions of yours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my conclusions were based on what I experienced and what I read afterwards and what I have read before. This was my opinion, written after I had left the ECM mission, and I had the right to have an opinion based on whatever. I don't think I had any reason to sit and explain here why I had this opinion when I came back home and was thinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, you have said this many times already. Apart from you, two monitors appeared before this Court who didn't stay longer on the ground than six or seven days. You are the only high-ranking official from the monitoring mission who can hopefully help us to portray the role, the terms of reference, and the workings of the mission in 1992 with reference to Dubrovnik, which is also the subject of this indictment. Because from your colleague Lars Brolund, we couldn't learn anything because he virtually couldn't remember anything; therefore, I'm kindly asking you to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to his speeches, Your Honour. There was no question there; it was nothing more than a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the position, Mr. Rodic. I think you can just move on to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree with my learned colleagues; there was no question. But this was just an intervention on my part with my line of questioning. Mr. Hvalkof --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say to you, Mr. Rodic, Mr. Weiner is being very patient and understanding. He's been to half to his feet more than once but he's sat down again. So you should appreciate how understanding he's being this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have noticed that myself, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, in paragraph 3 on the same page, the first sentence reads: "The ECMM was led by a Dutch ambassador and was for the most part under Dutch control." Under whose control were you?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mission was led during that period by Dutchmen as such, the head of mission and the heads, as far as I remember, of the various operations sections and headquarters in Zagreb were Dutchmen. And there were Dutch monitors among the rest of us out. So as a principle, the head of mission being a Dutchmen, Mr. Van Houten. He was the leader. So I was under the Dutch leadership. When I was in Split, I was under Italian leadership because my -- the head of the regional centre, Mr. Ambassador Bondioli, was an Italian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think we understood each other properly. When you say in the document that: "The mission was led by a Dutch ambassador and that the ambassador was for the most part under Dutch control," what does that mean, that he was under the Dutch control? Was he under control of his government, his Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the head of the mission was having -- conferring with his minister of foreign affairs who, at that time Holland had the chairmanship of the union, and that changes every six months. And whenever anything is under operation, in the European Union at that time -- the European Community at that time -- well, it will be the country who are chairing the mission or who is organising whatever of importance around the European Union, European Commission or Community. So it is natural that the ambassador confers with his government, and specifically with his minister of foreign affairs. And if it can help you, as head of the Danish mission, I had to refer to my minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time while you were working on the mission, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was working in the mission, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suppose that in that way individual countries could have exerted influence on the operation of their nationals posted with the mission?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not so. I have not in that mission, like the other ones I've been to, felt anything that the people I dealt with at all levels were neutral. And if we had been permitted to be moving freely on all sides, it would of course have been easier to prove to people that it was true we were neutral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yourself that you were under the control of the Danish minister of foreign affairs, that you contacted and consulted him while working for the mission. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to him or to the minister. I reported to them. All heads of mission reported directly also to their own minister of foreign affairs; it is quite normal and common. And that means that we reported briefly what the situation was or if there was something serious going on. We did not receive any orders from our minister of foreign affairs. We just informed them so they were in the picture so they knew what their own people were doing. Besides that, they were informed, to the best of my knowledge, I was anyway told so by the Dutch leadership, and that means apparently the Dutch minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic, or would you like -- did you have something you wanted to finish there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question in this context, and then we can proceed with the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me in your opinion during the two and a half months that you spent in Croatia, were opinions undivided and was there a single influence coming from all member states of the economic -- European Community regarding the situation on the ground in Yugoslavia, or were there any dissenting opinions from any particular country?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just read this, please. Well, it's a bit difficult for me to understand what you mean; language problem I believe. But if you -- the question goes on if we were sort of opinions which could indicate lack of neutrality was trying to be forced upon us or something like that, no, nothing. We were not influenced from our countries; we were reporting to our countries. We were not -- we were under command by the head of mission, a neutral and excellent man. And we were reporting -- there was no way of trying force -- everybody was extremely conscious of the fact that we had to be neutral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hvalkof.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we can now take a break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will -- yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was standing for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your eagerness took me by surprise. We will have our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, on page 2 of this statement under tab 42, you say in the second sentence that: "The basic philosophy was for the two parties or sides to negotiate on their own in solving their problems, whereas we acted as witnesses and helpers, what was necessary for someone to press the brakes, to push the things into the right direction, and to slam the fist on the table." Can you please explain for me in more detail this last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In some cases, situation discussions could become very heated. And then, somebody had to calm me down and say, That's going to be the end. We calmed down and talked in a decent way or get back to the point. So we're not talking about 200 years ago but now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in a position while you were with the mission to bang a fist on the table?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you escorted a convoy of the JNA leaving the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zagreb base Borongaj barracks?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the command team of that unit was at the rear of the column?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement in the brackets you said: "No comment." Can you please explain to me what that refers.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no comment to their -- why it was so. I still have no comments to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that one of the members of your monitoring team joined the command team of the JNA and that that is how he disappeared?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not join the command team of the JNA. He joined the team at the -- EC monitors at the rear vehicle of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 2 you say: "There were only two people in my team, one of whom had decided to join the team in command so he had disappeared." Was that referring to the command -- JNA command team that was at the rear of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who attacked the convoy and where this member of your monitoring team disappeared.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monitor member did not disappear; he went back and proceeded along with the convoy with the last vehicle in the convoy where the leaders of this operation were sitting and moving. Who attacked the convoy is -- well, we heard these shells coming down, which I mentioned en route, but who were flying I'm not in a position to see -- to tell. I have no clue. Some grenades landed en route. The blockade of the -- the artillery blockade in front of us when we reached Karlovac, I could not myself tell but I was informed that it was JNA by contacting my headquarters on -- I think it was a satellite phone we had along. But who attacked the convoy as such, if that was an attack close to the airport, I wouldn't know. And it was anyway not close to the convoy. It was just the end. And it didn't worry me much, but I noted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the JNA soldiers were nervous because there were Ustasha, as you say, in the area?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they were nervous but extremely well-behaved. But no wonder they were nervous; they were driving through territory controlled by people they didn't like. And there were -- we observed what we considered to be what I called Ustashas, as you mentioned before, a sort of, I understand, paramilitary forces. They were observed by us. I cannot confirm, but they were certainly in their general attitude. They were on Croatian territory and they didn't look -- or their movement seemed to be of a -- well, Croatian. They didn't misbehave, but you could observe them. And of course the JNA didn't like that, and they were sitting there peacefully being escorted by neutral people. So they were nervous, yes, quite natural. They were in a bad position if something happened and we couldn't stop it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will quote the way in which you called these Croatian soldiers Ustasha. In the next sentence you say: "The Ustasha were fanatic Croatian nationalists dressed in some sort of uniform with hand grenades in all their button holes with Indian hair styles or shaved heads, mostly with earrings, and they carried several pieces of infantry-type weapons, real Rambo types." Is this what you observed and thought?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw them, I saw them up close -- some of them on closer distance later. Yes, it was my final opinion. I was also briefed about other -- from other ECMM monitors who had met these people and this is maybe a bit of my humorous way of expressing myself, but also actually in a way of a sort -- the general opinion I got when I heard about -- when I heard these people and saw them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call the kind of people described here Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may be my pronunciation, whatever. That's what they were called in the area. I have no official remark about that. That's what they were called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you called them?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I called them that. I called them later on when I left the mission in this writing, but that -- but I didn't walk around calling people names so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We will now move on. On the 23rd of October you became the deputy head of the regional centre of the ECMM in Split which opened up on the 20th of October. Is this correct -- on the 28th of October --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th, that is correct. It was in full operation on the 28th, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Ambassador Bondioli the chief of your regional centre and did he have a meeting with General Strugar and Admiral Jokic on the 28th of October in Milejina [phoen] in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my chief and to the best of my knowledge, yes, he had a meeting down there if it was Milejina. He had a meeting with General Strugar down in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Lars Brolund also attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ambassador Bondioli acquaint you with the results of those talks?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. The way I remember them today best is according to the -- some of the notes or correspondence, which we talked about yesterday. But yes, he informed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what his impressions were of the people he had met, I mean primarily General Strugar and Admiral Jokic? Did he tell you what he observed about them?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said the meeting had gone well in that respect. No personal comments about persons -- about these two officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he perhaps mention that he experienced Admiral Jokic as a hard-liner and General Strugar as an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I've not heard that from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you about General Strugar's opinion that there should also be monitors on the JNA side so that they could also see the situation from the other side?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've not heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 23 there is Ambassador Bondioli's report, and the correction of dates is there. So it's not the 28th of November, but the 28th of October, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle of that report it says that the declaration of the European Community in Dubrovnik of the 27th of October was handed to General Strugar, the commander of the 2nd Military District in Milejina." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under that it says: "Apparently these two declarations together had a strong influence on the negotiating position of the JNA." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain the next sentence to me. "On the 28th, General Strugar sent an urgent message to the 20th meeting of the NOF in Brussels where he says that the 11 points of Dubrovnik are not an ultimatum."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember there was -- I've seen some -- the papers where General Strugar has put down 11 points. And as far as I remember, there was a discussion about this. And I can also remember this about the ultimatum, but I -- it's not -- I don't have it up to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the parts we have just read, do you get the impression and am I correct in saying that this -- these talks were correct and that they represented cooperation between Ambassador Bondioli and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no feeling that there was a bad atmosphere, the way I recall it, about this. There might have been, but it was not brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please distribute these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, yesterday you responded to questions by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, in connection with a correspondence between the JNA and the ECMM for the most part in connection with the 19th and 20th of October. Would you please, however, look at this letter written on the letterhead of the Argentina Hotel, dated the 17th of October, 1991, 1710. Could you please tell us what the content of this message is; the message was sent by Colonel Damjanovic to your mission in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just read it silently for yourself and tell us what the essential points are.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to have the second-last word in the second line explained. Is that boat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems to be.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, well as I see it, it is a complaint about transport of mortars between this name I can't read, but I think I know where it is, and Dubrovnik. And the two mortars, according to the Jeep man who was -- wrote this, have been brought in to repair -- bring mortars into position where they are not wanted. And that this is a warning to the ECMM to warn the crisis committee that this is not acceptable to the man who -- to the colonel or general who has written this. Yeah, I think that's the essential part of it. I have not seen this document before, and you may recall I was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not in Dubrovnik on the 19th and 20th of October either, and yet you explained documents from that period. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I cannot recall I have seen this piece of paper before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then explain to me why you saw only the reports of one side or only some of the reports, rather than gaining a complete picture about something you are talking about and interpreting. And yet you are not then present in Dubrovnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour, that's a misleading question. If you look at the four letters which came in, two are from the JNA and two are from -- to the JNA. That's a misleading questions. He saw reports from both sides yesterday in that period, prior to his being in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. My impression is that that is so, Mr. Rodic, and your question is to a degree misleading. I don't believe, though, that Mr. Hvalkof was misled, and he was in the process of answering. Would you like to continue, Mr. Hvalkof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I read all the information available during the time, but I cannot today in 2004 sit and remember all these details. What I can tell is what I had -- I'm sure of and what -- when I looked at my own notes from the time, because I know they were correct according to the way I saw the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The critical point you make, Mr. Hvalkof, is that you don't recall having ever seen this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't recall it, but I am sure I have. Because we were -- all these sort of things were filed, as I had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mentioned. But of course this could have happened. We didn't see it in Split, or what have you, when we came. We were starting up. It might have been missed somewhere, but I am sure I must have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the objection raised by my learned friend, but this is an introduction to the missing documentation which I will show to the witness and which I feel will alter the position with respect to the four letters he testified about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any investigation was undertaken by the European mission in connection with this, or whether the Crisis Staff was warned in connection with the contents of this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Anyway, I don't remember, but I'm sure that the crisis committee was warned by the ECMM team according to the message here. And I would presume if it operated the normal way down there at that time, they would have immediately investigated. But I cannot recall it, and it might have happened before I even showed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you saw a report by the monitors of the ECMM concerning any steps that might have been taken in connection with this by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you commented on a correspondence between the ECMM and the JNA, and these were four letters of the 19th and 20th of October, although you were not a direct participant because you were in Zagreb at the time. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 1, if you would be so kind as to take a look, please, there is a letter of protest dated the 19th of October, 1605 hours, sent from the mission to General Strugar in Kumbor. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this letter, the monitors ask that engineering units on the main road near Plat be withdrawn immediately, and it is claimed that they are entering into the defence positions of the other side. Do you know what engineers' units -- what the engineering units of the JNA were doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from what I read here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you explained that yesterday, only on the basis of this. But do you know what the JNA engineering units were doing, based on this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing more than what this letter states. I have no possibility of knowing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the other side was and to whose positions they were entering?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other side could only be the opposing party in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area you had two opposing parties: The JNA and the Croatian op forces, whatever they were called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the positions of this other side were, reading this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read the names. I cannot remember -- I had not been on the ground at the time. And at the time I was shown on the map, but it's -- that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they show you on the map? Did they show you something on the map in connection with this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know -- I've been briefed on maps several times about incidents. I cannot tell you any details about these briefings. I've seen maps. Now they are here, now the line is there, et cetera. That's all I can answer you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me why this is seen as a provocative act by the ECMM? And to assist you I will tell you that they were repairing the road.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can only be a guess. To repair a road could mean that you achieve an advantage by being able to move weapons, equipment, et cetera, forward or whatever. But it's only a guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can only guess now in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps that on that same day, the 19th of October, an hour before sending this protest note to Kumbor at 1455 you received an explanation of the activities of the JNA in relation to the disinformation from the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff, with whom you had good cooperation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you say I received; I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before we distribute this next document, could this one at least be either marked for identification or listed as an exhibit so in the future we'll know what we're referring to with various documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I take it you have no objection to it being received as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The letter or the note dated 18th October 1991 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number will be D25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to have the date as 1981. I take it we're all happy that it should be 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says 19th October 1991 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the contents of this letter which you say did not reach ECMM monitors before they sent the letter to Kumbor at 1605 hours.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was not there; I did not receive it. Now I will read it. I might have read it before. I have read it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this letter addressed to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik and members of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 14th of October at 1455 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, at 1455 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was signed by Captain Jeremic as a representative of the JNA staff in Kumbor, Boka?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like the signature, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this letter, did the JNA explain that their units were either advancing or going forward, that the units in the Plat area were engineers that were just working on the road repairs that you had blown up, and that they primarily pleaded with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik as well as with the ECMM to give them time and opportunity to repair this road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by the sequence in time, was this letter sent before the ECMM sent a warning to General Strugar in Kumbor at 1605 hours?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This apparently was sent before, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this report, or rather, this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't remember this letter as well, just like the previous one?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask for this document to be given a Defence number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said that you don't remember either of those letters marked with D25 and D26, can you tell me the -- if you must have read, just as you must have read these other letters?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I must have read them, yes. I have not seen them since that time. The rest of the letters I have been talking about I have seen later than that time, the ones we talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were briefed for -- during the conversation, were you selectively shown these letters?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was briefed, it was verbal; when I was reading, I got a file of papers and was reading through. When you read through files, I'm not a lawyer like you, but I read through at the time and I don't remember 14 years or 13 years later what I read in detail at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were an impartial observer in 1991, testifying now, and therefore you should also be impartial in your testimony speaking about facts and events as they actually happened, particularly if the facts are well-argumented. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible then that this letter sent at 1455 hours, given the time of the meeting and the content of the very letter, and I'm referring to the letter from tab 1, was not given to the ECMM by the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff in time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, you're asking the witness to speculate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is well-founded. The answer is being given and it's a dead-neutral answer. So we will move on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one say that the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff was raising tensions, and that that was condoned by the ECMM members through this letter dated 19th October?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you now think that the repair works on the road damaged by the Croatian units could be qualified as a provocation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not know. Maybe it could, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this letter sent by the ECMM, there is a demand for General Strugar to immediately withdraw his engineer units near Plat. Doesn't that mean then that those -- the authors of this letter knew the contents of the letter D26 that I just presented to you, and in which it was explained what the engineers units had been doing?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I don't have that letter, again it was brought up. It doesn't matter. The point is that whatever they knew or not, the neutral team in a position like this must convey all messages passed from either side when they are asked to do so. You may sit and disagree, but when the party says, Would you pass that message, you pass it. And I believe that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ECMM letter referring to the withdrawal of the JNA engineers units was written in a rather commanding manner?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I now please ask you to have a look at tab 2. It's a letter dated 19th of October. The time was 1825. It was sent to General Strugar by the ECMM. So if you look at this letter, it seems to me that this is of an identical content with tab 5; therefore, it's the same letter. But above the name of General Strugar, you can see that it was actually sent by Colonel Svicevic and addressed to General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're still talking about tab 3, aren't we -- or tab 2, sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, tab 2. And in tab 4, there is an identical document to this one. I apologise. I made a mistake when I said "tab 5." So tabs 2 and 4 contain the same document, but in tab 4 in the left upper corner of the letter, one can discern that it was sent to -- it was sent through Colonel Svicevic for General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot read what is above -- or I can't -- for General Strugar. I'll have to trust what you're saying. I can't read it. I see half the letters are cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but I think that my colleague, the Prosecutor, shares my opinion. In your further response to the Prosecution's question, you also gave your explanation of this letter sent to Colonel Svicevic and to the attention of General Strugar. Is it true that in this letter, the ECMM has become more involved in the political situation? For instance, in paragraph 2, the second sentence of this letter.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: So is that the question? Okay. The letter was not made by me, but to me it is quite natural that when you work as a neutral organisation, in this case -- sorry, for the ECMM, it is quite natural to point out that the -- what they are doing here. There is nothing unnormal compared to all the other places I have been. You frequently have to point this sort of thing out to all the involved parties.
