And it just says, for example: All armed forces, all armed forces, that's on both sides if that's the sort of thing you're referring to. So me, that is nothing wrong; it's natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to the -- from the beginning of the letter up to the sentence you have just read. Are these the positions and views of the ECMM in which they were explaining the political situation to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who wrote this, I cannot vouch for what he's writing. But the way I see it is that he is trying to explain how he and his team is feeling the situation is. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you consider that these are appropriate views presented by the ECMM to one of the sides, in this case to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I have nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then tell me what does this sentence mean, I quote: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Concerning the -- as far as the Dubrovnik area is concerned, the EC monitoring mission has been informed by the people that they did not call on the JNA." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The way I read it is that they did not call the JNA -- they did not ask the JNA to approach Dubrovnik. But I can't vouch for it. I did not read it -- I didn't write it, but that is obvious to me. And the monitors are bringing the views of the other party across as well as when they came back from meetings were bringing your -- the JNA views, across to the crisis committee or town council or whatever. So this is the way I -- and that was the way we worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which people it was that said that they had not called on the JNA? Who told you that anyway?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me. I said I was not there. You asked me to give a remark about this, and this is the EC monitor's mission personnel down in Dubrovnik at the time who have written this. And I can't give you a fair answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us make it clear. When I asked you who told you, I wasn't referring to you personally, because I know you weren't there. But you interpreted the views of other members of the mission who wrote this. Could it be that it was said to the monitors by the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been the only way it could have appeared, that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you read this, do you think that this language and tone assumed by the monitoring mission and the formulation of sentences as such is a correct way that reflects your impartiality?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To bring information from one side to the other as actually requested from one of the sides, in the way in the tone it was expressed is a correct way of behaving and has got nothing to do with the impartiality. And I consider this, the way I read it, they are passing information in the tone it was given to them, and that's a fair way of passing the information to your side. It does not express - when you do this sort of thing - anything about what is happening inside the neutral monitor's mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that this letter is nothing to do with being a messenger conveying a message, but rather of lecturing and giving orders and it is in connection with the previous letter you had agreed was written in a sort of a commanding manner. Is that correct? This is not the way to explain the situation in Yugoslavia to General Strugar by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your opinion. I think it's a fair way of passing information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we proceed, please. Was the role of the monitors to judge whether the Yugoslav People's Army in its own territory, because at the time there was yet no political solution and the author of this letter has stepped beyond the role -- the limits of your mandate, siding with one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to talk to him about it. I didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But yesterday you were prepared or willing to testify to this letter and to give your interpretation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me to give interpretation today; I've done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go down through the content. The monitors say to the general that: "You should realise that after 19 days of fighting the repairment [as interpreted] of the road in the defensive position of the commune of Dubrovnik can only be regarded as an aggressive act, contrary to the confidence you are appealing on in the message of 1710 hours today, signed by Colonel Svicevic. We therefore again stress strongly that you have to withdraw behind your own lines." Can you explain this to me, this interpretation given by your colleagues, that repair works on the road in the defensive position of the commune of Dubrovnik can only be regarded as an aggressive act. Can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have done it before, but they are passing messages from the other side. They might have observed something themselves, which I can't say. I wasn't there. I don't know who wrote it. But, as I say, they passed messages. And we had been passing messages the other way around, or they had for sure about remarks, maybe in a harsh tone given from both sides. And that is what is happening here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that we can agree that this sentence carries no message. It is rather that the monitor is persuading the general what he should realise. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the eyes who looks at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me then what -- how can repair works on the road constitute an aggressive act?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again as I did before - and I don't want to talk directly about this thing - but repair of works -- of roads may mean that it's easier to move equipment and troops ahead. I have met many other cases and other missions with repair of roads in areas, in front line areas, where there was a hell of a lot -- sorry about my blunt language, where there were a lot of problems caused. And to me, this is just the some -- the same sort of thing here. And I have got no further comments on this one; I can't give further comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean in this particular case that the monitoring mission sees road repair works as an aggressive act? Let me rephrase. Does not the mission see this as an aggressive act or -- and does it only convey an opinion that it constitutes an aggressive act?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's their right of -- it's their duty to pass a message. If they get an information that one side is finding this an aggressive act, they should pass it. And that's a part of the job, so they do so. If you don't tell the opposite party that you find it an aggressive act, it may escalate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't see this an aggressive act, rather that was a message from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I say the repairing of roads could be aggressive acts, and these people consider it to be an aggressive act. And that's why they're asking the message to be passed. That's why repair -- the way I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, which sounds as an order to withdraw behind the lines, was that referring to the engineers units working on the road repair works?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: EC monitors don't give orders -- they didn't give orders. And neutral observers in missions like that don't give orders but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it simply mean that the Crisis Staff was issuing order to General Strugar through the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were issuing orders -- I don't see it as orders. If you consider it to be an order -- well, to me they are passing messages of worries of some nature. And the ECM mission people are forwarding them to you, and bad luck if you find it's an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which members of the mission were in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, or rather, can you can sure that the monitors from the mission team in Dubrovnik at the time in the hotel, were they in the hotel at the time? Were they in a cafe? Or were they walking around the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can't be sure. I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another important point: You persist in speaking about the transmission of messages of one side, the Croatian side, to the other, the JNA. Is it correct that it is your messages, due to problems in communication, the messages that you sent out or received in the mission, that they all went through the Croatian side. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. Because messages you pass to the mission went through the mission channels. But when the Croats, for example, asked us to pass a message to you, we did it. If you had done the same, we would have done that. But we did not pass messages for us to them, no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any direct connection with the staff in Kumbor, in Boka, the JNA staff there?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're giving me a knew name I don't know. I have not heard about Kumbor before. And when are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 1, the letter which you testified about is addressed to General Pavle Strugar in Kumbor. Do you know where Kumbor is?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To me it looks like Dumbar, I'm sorry, and actually I thought misreading, it meant Dubrovnik. I've never been aware of that. But I didn't -- I can't read that word. But -- so -- and I don't know where Kumbor is, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's addressed to General Strugar in Kumbor by the monitors from your mission. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's addressed to General Strugar, that's correct. It's from the mission -- from the ECM monitor team, yes, that is correct. I have never been worried about the name, whatever, it's Boka or something else. I knew it was Croatian -- or sorry, JNA territory. And we were not actually concerned -- informed and really concerned about where your various headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which staff? Whose headquarters, that is?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is addressed to Pavle Strugar, General, so personally I did not know where the general was sitting on his daily desk, and that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the monitors then have addressed a letter to him in Ljubljana, for example?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were talking about addressing letters and messages to the officer in command of the JNA forces in the Dubrovnik area. And I know that sometimes we were talking about Boka. Now you are mentioning another name. There has been meetings in Miljenje. Where the general's exact headquarters -- or if he had more, which is most likely, other places, I don't know. We are talking about passing messages to the senior JNA officer in the Dubrovnik area, and the exact name of the office or the place was no interest to me at the time and it still is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters, or rather, the command post of Admiral Jokic was?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not ask the question. I have met the admiral, and it was not important for me to know that. It was important to me what happened and what action people took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In this letter there is mention of a message signed by Colonel Svicevic at 1710, and that is in tab 2. Is this correct? Tab 2 or 4, it's the same letter.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 2, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are you familiar with the content of Colonel Svicevic's letter at 1710, which is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just enlighten me so I can find that through the script with my old eyes where this is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry at the bottom. Would you repeat the question now, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you personally familiar with the content of the -- contained in Colonel Svicevic's letter, and did you have an opportunity to see it study it before testifying about this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember I've seen that better I came down here. Right now I can't, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not show you this letter, and it is missing from the file, just like the other one sent by Captain Jeremic. Isn't that so? D26, I mean.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which file are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: D26 is not in the tab. It is rather a Defence exhibit introduced today. The letter sent at 1455 hours by Captain Jeremic addressed to the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the letters which was shown before. I don't have it here. It's given back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: The letter that you looked at you said you hadn't seen before. I'm now asking you: Did you see Colonel Svicevic's letter of 1710? Did you see it when you were being briefed for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you're referring now -- I don't have it front of me. You're referring to the piece of paper, the letters, which you distributed before, I have not seen them before in connection with this arrangement here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the letter sent by Captain Jeremic and is it correct that you did not see it when preparing for your testimony and that it preceded the first protest letter from tab 1, which was addressed to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it in connection with the trial, before today. I'm sure I've seen it many years ago, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, is that last letter Exhibit D25, the one the witness has just commented on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is D26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter sent by Captain Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, do you understand that yesterday you testified, and today I am asking you in connection with tab 1 and 2. These are letters sent by the ECMM to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Exhibit 1, there is a letter at 1605 hours. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just shown you a letter from Captain Jeremic sent at 1455, which you did not see before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I am asking you in relation to this second letter from tab 2, during your proofing did you see the letter that was sent at 1710 by Colonel Svicevic to the ECMM, which preceded this letter from the ECMM sent at 1825? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said my briefing. Are you talking about the briefing in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were handed these tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen these tab numbers here. The documents you have produced today I have not seen here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about these documents in tabs 1 and 2 where you were not a direct participant or the author of these documents, shouldn't you be neutral, as a former monitor, and ask to see, for example, the letter sent by Colonel Svicevic at 1705, which is mentioned in tab 2?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been asked to tell the truth, and the truth, and I have been presented with these things. I've answered questions. If I had to ask questions about all the other documents and conversations happening in 1991, I would probably be here for a long time. I have answered what I have been asked as well as I could. And it has got nothing to do with my neutrality in 1991 or in this case. And I don't want that to be doubted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you when you say this. Is it possible, in view of the fact that at the time you did not participate in drawing up these letters and that you were not present in Dubrovnik, that through this selective presentation of ECMM documents you might be misused, unconsciously, in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't feel I've been misused. I've tried to do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without reading Colonel Svicevic's letters, can you say now that the standpoints put forward in the mission letters in tab 2 are correct and proper and that you were not misled now by the Prosecutor and in the past by the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I don't remember and don't know the letter; I can't ask for it and I had no reason to ask for it. When you have two opposing parties sending arguments, of course they have very different opinions about the situations. When you pass the messages, you try to discuss it at meetings, you try to solve the problems, that you might have a bit of a -- is nothing of value. I can't say anything more to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher please distribute this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Issue there, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the same issue. I am introducing a new document in connection with these letters, in order to resolve the situation with the assistance of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let's hope we can do it fairly quickly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document be given an exhibit number right away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see it already has an identification number. Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, have you acquainted yourself now with the content of this letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not show you this letter before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me on the basis of, what when you read this letter, would the monitors from your mission, those who were in Dubrovnik, be able to reject this letter from Colonel Svicevic. How could they justify that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you read this, do you consider that the repair of the road for the needs of the situation in the JNA was an act of aggression, as mentioned in the letter in tab 2?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the spot -- the situation on the ground before I said anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the monitors did anything in connection with a protest against the violation of the cease-fire that is contained in Colonel Svicevic's letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they carried out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the monitors did because the Croatian forces were carrying out movements, as indicated in Colonel Svicevic's letter?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I know that the normal procedure is, if possible, you're not risking your lives, you carry out an investigation on the spot, and I know that you negotiate and pass messages to try to calm the situation down. What they did at the time, I still can't answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know whether they did anything about the new arming in certain locations mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are talking about the time before I came. I concentrated and there was enough to concentrate on what was happening from the time I arrived, what the situation was like. And that was enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that regardless of the fact that you were not in Dubrovnik, you read the reports from Dubrovnik, the correspondence and the reports from your mission. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was available. You may take into consideration that these people who were down in Dubrovnik, whatever was there, it might have arrived at a time in -- when I was on the move down or later. Anyway, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cannot remember all these papers; I can't. I can remember what I had personally and what I had been presented with. I say, Oh, yeah, I've seen that before. This -- the majority of what I presented for you is something I had myself. This one I don't have, it's something that showed up before my presence. I don't have it. And when you read stacks of papers, anyway, if you were me, you wouldn't be able to remember all of it in detail so many years after. You wouldn't. What I read myself and what I -- surely matters I've handled myself, yes, I think I could, when I look at it again, remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that conclude that line of questioning, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, or rather, a few questions in connection with this, because I will speak about a new exhibit from the tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be good to have a break now, and I think your client would like that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, please look at tab number 5. This is a letter sent by General Strugar to the monitoring mission, bearing the date of 20th of October and the time is 1945. This is a letter which is a reply to the letter from the ECMM of the 19th of October in tab 4; that is the letter we were discussing before the break. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you look at the content of this letter, can we agree that it is a polite reply, in spite of the tone used in the letters of the ECMM of the 19th of October at 1605 and 1825?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a polite reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Especially if we bear in mind that General Strugar had information, the information transmitted by Captain Jeremic to the ECMM in connection with the engineers' units and what they were doing and the information Colonel Svicevic also transmitted to the ECMM, while in reply he received from the ECMM letters numbered tabs 1 and 2. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see now that the observers in Dubrovnik were manipulated - you were not there - because they did not have the entire scope of communication in the letters?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the letter and I agree. I have nothing against the tone of the letter. I cannot confirm anything about monitors being manipulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will remind you that yesterday, when questioned by the Prosecutor about this letter, the one before you now, tab 5, you said you did not like the tone in which it was written, although you were not in Dubrovnik at the time. I believe, however, that now after having seen the JNA documents sent to the monitoring mission, which you did not have an opportunity of seeing before, you have changed your opinion. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think -- know if I have changed my opinion, but if I look at it now it doesn't sound that bad. And anyway, I have nothing against a sharp tone in a letter as such; I'll have to accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that we may be assisted here by another letter of the 20th of October sent at 1950, which is in tab number 6. Would you please now look at the content of this letter. That means that between 1300 hours and 1900 hours on the 19th of October, despite the cease-fire, the JNA suffered the loss of three men and had a number of wounded. However, in that period, the mission had sent these previously-discussed two letters. Can we now understand better General Strugar's letter from tab 5?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can easily understand the general's words about losing people. That's of course very important. Yes, I can understand that. To me this is again a normal document. Of course you are complaining about something you don't like and you find is wrong, yes, I understand that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it proper that while the cease-fire was in force between 1500 and 1800 hour on the 19th of October, the JNA suffered the loss of three men and had 17 wounded men, while at the same time the mission sent a letter ordering the engineers units to be withdrawn because they were performing an act of aggression. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is always wrong when a cease-fire is broken. I cannot answer for what the EC monitor mission team in Dubrovnik were doing and where they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I fully agree with you on that, because I asked you a similar question before the break. Now can you please look carefully at tab 7 and read it. This is the letter sent by the mission to Captain Jeremic for which I claim to be a completely different one in terms of its tone from the ones sent to General Strugar on the 19th of October. I believe we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to read it first. Yeah, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we in agreement that the tone of this letter is completely different to the tone present in the letter sent by the mission on the 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's different, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, the mission expressed its regret of not receiving the letter sent to Captain Jeremic and referring to the postponement of a meeting? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the solution of this correspondence on the 20th and the 19th of October between the mission be perceived from item 2 of this letter, where the mission observers say that they relied or depended on Dubrovnik radio to transmit their messages to the JNA and that there was no other way of communicating with them, they also said that "like you mention people misused this line of communication and it is unfortunately out of our control." Is that the key to this whole body of correspondence?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the key, but it's a possibility, of course, when communications are bad and you have to use the means available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it only enough that the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik failed to convey the messages between the mission and the JNA, and that that could have resulted in misunderstandings?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the mission who drafted this letter precisely speak about this under item 2, and that that is they depended on their communications on Radio Dubrovnik and that they had no other channels to communicate other than that one?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they write. I trust that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in -- with respect to this letter, one more issue, and that is pertaining to item 3. I think that we can agree that the tone of addressing the recipient is completely different than the one used in the letters dated 19th of October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tone is different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please ask you now to move to tab 3. This document is entitled "The Interpretation of the Current Cease-fire in Dalmatia." When you look at this document, can you tell me: Is it sort of an analysis and who has prepared this analysis and based on what?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see -- I can remember I've seen this document before. It -- to me it is an analysis. And who wrote it, I cannot remember. And I don't even know -- I'll have to see but I'm not sure. But it is an analysis made by ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 5 of this document entitled "Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to me what did this conclusion at the beginning of the second sentence which reads that: "Dubrovnik itself has no military or strategic value," and who was able to arrive at such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who wrote this arrived at this conclusion, and I expressed yesterday that I sort of had the same feeling myself. But that's analysed by this person, and of course you don't always discuss that. Anyway, that has no influence on the work you do, that you might feel this. You do the work of negotiating with people, investigating, and handling the matters on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I know, this type of analysis and reports are normally forwarded to your headquarters in Zagreb and from then on to the ambassadors of the EC member countries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally it would be forwarded to headquarters of Zagreb. And now I -- I don't know, but this to me seems like the paper made in Zagreb, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When anyone in the European Community receiving such reports from monitoring missions made conclusions about the prevailing situation in Yugoslavia, could they do that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what -- how -- what conclusion they made out of reading this. How should I know what they do and what they think?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you inform from the ground anyone in Europe by stating that Dubrovnik itself has no military or strategic value, what could anyone in Paris, Brussels, Frankfurt, or Copenhagen conclude from that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't state anything at the time about that. So you will have the people sitting then evaluating this like you evaluate any intelligence information. I don't know how they do -- how they evaluated this. You get opinions. You have to discuss them, find other sources and that sort of stuff. But I have had nothing to do with it. So I don't know what they do and where they ended up and that was the result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more thing about this particular sentence. If we bear in mind that Dubrovnik was in the territory of the SFRY, that the SFRY as a country had its own strategy of defence and evaluation of territories that it deems of importance and especially if it is unknown what the tasks of the JNA second operations groups were, then we can conclude that this kind of conclusion can be very pretentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Number one, there's no timing on that. Number two, it's an issue for this Court to determine under whose authority the city of Dubrovnik was. They've indicated if we bear in mind that it was under the JNA -- I'm sorry, in the territory of the SFRY and the SFRY had its own strategy of defence. Then he's asking him about the conclusion can be very pretentious. The question has no meaning, number one. Number two, it's an issue of international law. And number three, I don't think it's relevant for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, page 1, has the logo or the mark of the ECMM and it's dated the 24th of October, 1991. And irrespective of the comments of my learned friend, I believe that the area of Dubrovnik could be deemed to be more in the context of the SFRY than in the crisis situation that is being discussed here under the indictment against General Strugar. And I don't see any relevance of that to the question that I asked the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As all counsel are well aware, it will be for this Chamber at the end to determine issues such as the status of Dubrovnik and what, in fact, was occurring politically at the time, and in particular whether or not there was an international conflict affecting the relevant events. What you put to the witness, Mr. Rodic, was very much in the line of one of your statements rather than a question and was very loaded with that type of international law element so that it becomes, A, impossible for a witness such as Mr. Hvalkof to answer it; and in any event it's not for a witness such as Mr. Hvalkof but for this Chamber. So I must uphold the objection of Mr. Weiner, and if you would move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In continuation of this evaluation about the situation in Dubrovnik, it is stated that there were no significant Croatian forces in the area, there was no heavy weaponry there other -- only small arms and perhaps some anti-tank guns. Do you share this opinion, since you in your capacity as the deputy head of the regional centre were active in Dubrovnik and were personally visiting this territory?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any heavy weapons, so I agree with this, and I have no reports of heavy weapons. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your definition of heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my definition would say heavy weaponry is above 81-millimetre mortars. I have met people who consider 81-millimetre mortars heavy weapons, too. However, I did not see any of those in the area and I have no report about heavy weapons -- anyway not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the commander of the defence of the City of Dubrovnik as well as many other witnesses said that there were 120-millimetre mortars in Dubrovnik, that there was a variety of guns, how would you assess that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's his statement. But I can't confirm they were there. So I have to stick to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the 116th ZNG Brigade was in the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of the unit. I don't know the name of the unit, but I know there were Croatian armed forces in the area. But I don't know the numbers and the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more precisely which area are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Dubrovnik area -- I knew there were small forces around the town of Dubrovnik itself. And to the best of my knowledge, there were forces up -- Croatian forces up at Stan which is up en route towards -- not too far away towards Split. And I recall fighting in the Stan area with JNA and Croatian forces. But the -- I never saw personally -- you have to consider my own short stay in Dubrovnik. I never saw really armed personnel in Dubrovnik, and I never saw any weapons in Dubrovnik. And I didn't worry about the number of the unit they -- I can never recall I ever heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to say that there was no Croatian forces in Dubrovnik and no Croatian artillery and that they did not operate from within Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said I didn't see it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard there were Croatian forces deployed in Dubrovnik and that there were Croatian artillery weapons operating from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've heard not about the weapons. There were some sort of Croatian forces, armed personnel, in and around Dubrovnik. Yes, I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If anything else -- had you ever heard from members of your monitoring team and through their reports learned about the positions and operations of the Croatian army and artillery from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about small arms firing from -- I think it was called the Fort Mount Srdj. Is that correct? I cannot recall details about anything else, and I have -- say again that my impression was that the Croatian forces in the Dubrovnik area were very small and armed with small-arms weapons. And when you tell me what I've seen, I have told you already what I have seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me on the basis of what do you assert that you know they had only light weapons, that there were few of them, and that the Croatian forces fired from Srdj only from light weapons.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that my information about the forces I got from the monitors down there. I did not say they only fired with light arms from Srdj, but that -- what I saw myself was very little, but then I saw something which sounded -- looked like machine gun fire on the 6th, and that was a very short, brief, minute. That's all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from the monitors in your mission that fire was opened from artillery pieces in Dubrovnik; for example, Boskovic park between the Belvedere Hotel and the Excelsior Hotel, from near the Argentina Hotel, where the ECM monitors were put up, and similar locations. Were you able to see this from their reports?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not report anything like that to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they forbidden -- were they banned from reporting on this?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. They had to report everything. They would report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How then do you explain that witnesses who testified before this Tribunal mentioned such things?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can I answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He can't comment on the credibility or another persons' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or on their observation, which was not the observation of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is one that is misplaced, Mr. Rodic, for the reasons that have been canvassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time of your mission in Dubrovnik or in connection with Dubrovnik, did you ever have contacts with the Croatian army, regardless of their numbers, that is with the commanders of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dealt with the crisis committee. One of the members was wearing a camouflage uniform. I was not -- I was dealing with them as a crisis committee, and as the leaders or the assistants, whatever you'd like to call it, of Dubrovnik. But that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of this member of the crisis committee who wore a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I have no clue. I might have talked to them if he was accompanying them. He could have been a security guard; I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have information to the effect that it was the crisis committee that was at the head of the Croatian army, of course I mean in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the top Croatian authorities we were negotiates with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by the top Croatian authorities? I'm asking you specifically did the Croatian army take orders from the Crisis Staff in the Dubrovnik area, or did they have their own command?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you that we were discussing all matters of the people we had there concerning the situation around Dubrovnik and what happened on the Croatian side. That was discussed, to the best of my knowledge, with the crisis committee concerning military and civilian matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the Crisis Staff that made all important decisions, because they were the ones you were in contact with. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. We were -- they were the ones we discussed with, and they were the leaders of the Croats in the area to our understanding and -- but I can't answer the other part of your question. How should I know?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you not at all interested in the Croatian army in the Dubrovnik area as one of the sides, the JNA being other side? So if the JNA was one side, the Croatian army was supposed to be the other side. And as you explained, the goal of the mission was to mediate between those two sides. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the Croatian army then? You know nothing about one of the sides?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever -- of course we were -- whatever -- there were of Croatian forces. The main impression and what I recall the monitors who were there and actually moved around in the area, which I didn't, was that it was very small light-armed forces of a not very much regular army type. You could compare with a bit of fighting resistance if I can use that word comparison to the Second World War where you had something like that in many places including Yugoslavia. It didn't seem to be very well organised and it didn't seem to be professional people to the best of my knowledge. That was what people reported. I didn't see them myself. There was no time during my two visits to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With all due respect, I think you've gone too far in your portrayal going as far as back as World War II. However, what I'm asking you specifically is: If there is a problem on the ground in Dubrovnik and the JNA complains and addresses a protest to your mission saying that the cease-fire had been violated and that a JNA soldier had been killed, for example, who then do you turn to to transmit this message and possibly launch a protest?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You turn in this case to the crisis committee. And the normal thing to then do would be to try to investigate the matter and then insist that if they carried out something like that where you have a JNA soldier killed, anything which could be doing harm to the other side, to inform them that they have to stop this thing if that is happening. But first of all when the protest comes in, you bring it to -- you pass the information in this case to the leaders of the resistance in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the leaders of the resistance in Dubrovnik, that was the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have mentioned that that was my general opinion. Now and then and together with them, you also had the -- we were talking to the mayor of Dubrovnik. If he was also a member of the crisis committee or talking on -- as a town council, I'm not sure. But they were working closely together, and they were the leaders in the area we were talking to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: You said you had contacts with, among others, General Mladenic in Split. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what General Mladenic's position was?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed he was the commander of the naval base, Lora base, in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will tell you that General Mladenic -- I withdraw the question. You said and mentioned that you talked to General Raseta in Zagreb. Can you tell me what his position was, where does he belong?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I did not talk to General Raseta. I have never seen the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any letters addressed to him by the ECMM? Was he ever sought out or asked to intervene?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in this bunch of paper his name appears. And in connection with any specific case, you'll have to show me the paper. But I remember his name, but I had nothing to do with the man personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember everything only when you have before you documents that you can look at?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember case -- things where I was involved personally. And when you want me to get into what was written at what time at a certain date, I require, due to the many years ago it happened, to look. And I know the things I have written myself, messages I have received myself, I know that I wrote down what was the truth at the time. And you're trying to ask me about lots of pieces of paper I have had no actual dealing, which I find is unfair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. All right. Admiral Jokic, what do you know about him? What was he?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out he was a vice-admiral. It was the impression I had that he was attached to General Strugar. I have no idea of how the actual set-up was, but he was anyway representing the JNA at the meeting I attended, the two meetings, in Cavtat. And a vice-admiral is a very senior officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the commander of a military formation? Did you have this information?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion he would be when he is sent out to negotiate with two Croatian ministers, it's most likely. But nobody informed me what his exact job -- what he was at. There was no doubt that the three Croatian ministers found that he was a man high-ranking enough to negotiate at that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, you do not know now what exactly the position of Vice-Admiral Miodrag Jokic was and of what he was the commander at the time in October and December 1991, while you were dealing with Dubrovnik. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct I do not know his appointment -- I did not know his appointment. But when he is sent out as a representative negotiating with three ministers, I presume that he is an important person. But nobody told me about his exact appointment in his unit or his staff or wherever he came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you that your monitors who were in Dubrovnik and who had more frequent communication with Admiral Jokic knew and reported on his appointment, both to the regional centre of your mission and to the main centre in Zagreb. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. They did that. They passed the information they had. You'll find in this book also there is a note somewhere stating that the people they were negotiating with in Dubrovnik were first General Strugar, secondly Admiral Jokic. I think then Captain Jeremic, and then there was some other people. And you assume from that list that you have the people ranking in the order they are in command in the area. That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What was General Strugar's appointment?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in general he was mentioned as the commander of the Croatian forces -- or sorry, I'm very sorry, of the JNA in the Dubrovnik area. As also mentioned, I recall, we have looked at that paper today, about the commander -- the commander and chief of the Military District number 2 as far as I remember. But the majority of information stated that the general was in command of the JNA in the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the JNA formation in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have got no exact information about the specific units, their numbers, et cetera. But there was no doubt that there was JNA units around Dubrovnik. And I cannot -- if I have heard, I cannot remember the number of units and what they were called, et cetera. But they were there for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me General Kadijevic, what was his appointment?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was -- now, names are difficult, but I think he was the minister of defence, or equivalent to what you may call it in your country, and sitting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct in connection with all these names, Mladenic, Raseta, Jokic, and Strugar, that either you personally or other representatives of your mission addressed them on various occasions, most often in writing, and all in connection with the situation around Dubrovnik? Kadijevic too, of course.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mission might have had conversations, meetings with Mladenic. Raseta I believe, I can't confirm it. Jokic I know for sure. Strugar I know for sure. And personally I know that I have sent messages in writing to Mladenic, General Mladenic, Admiral Jokic, and General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any messages to General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said anyone from the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've run out of time, Mr. Rodic. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I wanted to round off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you were going to say your cross-examination there for a moment. We must be getting nearer the end, though, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honour, I cannot make you happy in this way, but I will do my best tomorrow. And I believe that I will be finished in the first session tomorrow. I'll do my very best to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I give a remark? I need to be back at my farm Friday morning latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we show every sign of your evidence finishing in the course of tomorrow morning. And I would suggest you arrange a flight at the latest time you can tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will live in prayer until then. We will adjourn now until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: at 1.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 25
